details:
**"Unfinished" Symphony (Symphony No. 8 in B minor, D. 759)**
Schubert's most famous symphony, begun in 1822 and left with only two complete movements, though a third-movement scherzo survives in sketches. Its 3/4 first movement opens with a dark, quiet melody in the cellos and basses (B, C-sharp, D, B) before an oboe and clarinet theme enters, and its second movement is an Andante con moto in E major. It was not premiered until 1865, decades after his death.

**"Erlkönig" ("The Erlking")**
Schubert's setting of Goethe's ballad about a father riding through the night with his sick son, who is lured and finally killed by the supernatural Erlking. The piano's relentless octave triplets depict the galloping horse, and a single singer portrays four characters: narrator, father, son, and Erlking.

**Trout Quintet (Piano Quintet in A major)**
A chamber work for the unusual ensemble of piano, violin, viola, cello, and double bass, so it has only one violin. Its fourth movement is a set of variations on Schubert's song "Die Forelle" ("The Trout"), whose rising piano sextuplets depict the fish leaping in the stream.

**Winterreise**
Schubert's song cycle setting 24 poems by Wilhelm Müller about a rejected lover's bleak winter journey. It opens with "Gute Nacht," includes "Der Lindenbaum" (The Linden Tree), "Die Wetterfahne" (a creaking weathervane), "Die Post" (a posthorn call), and "Irrlicht" (Will-o'-the-Wisp), and ends with "Der Leiermann" (The Hurdy-Gurdy Man), whose left hand repeats a drone-like open fifth.

**Die schöne Müllerin**
Schubert's earlier song cycle on Wilhelm Müller poems about a journeyman miller who falls in love with a miller's daughter. It opens with "Das Wandern," uses a constant repeated F-sharp in "Die liebe Farbe" to show his obsession with the color green, and ends with the brook singing a lullaby after he drowns himself in it.

**Rosamunde entr'acte**
Schubert wrote incidental music for Helmina von Chézy's play Rosamunde, Princess of Cyprus. Its B minor entr'acte is often theorized to be the intended finale of the Unfinished Symphony, and a Rosamunde theme also appears in his String Quartet No. 13 in A minor, the "Rosamunde" Quartet.

**Death and the Maiden**
A lied setting Matthias Claudius's poem in which Death comforts a frightened girl. Schubert used it as the theme for variations in the slow movement of his String Quartet No. 14 in D minor (D. 810), written in 1824 after his syphilis diagnosis; the quartet is known for sudden dynamic contrasts and ends with a tarantella.

**"Great" C major Symphony (Symphony No. 9)**
Schubert's longest symphony, called "Great" to distinguish it from his "Little" Sixth Symphony in the same key. It opens with two unison horns playing a motto theme, uses a three-key exposition (C major, E minor, G major), and was premiered posthumously by Felix Mendelssohn after Robert Schumann, who praised its "heavenly length," discovered the manuscript.

**"Gretchen am Spinnrade" ("Gretchen at the Spinning Wheel")**
An early lied setting a scene from Goethe's Faust, in which Gretchen sings "My peace is gone, my heart is heavy" while longing for Faust. The piano's whirling figures depict the spinning wheel and a foot treadle, and the motion stops abruptly when she recalls his kiss ("sein Kuss!").

**"Ave Maria" ("Ellens dritter Gesang")**
"Ellen's Third Song," part of Schubert's Op. 52 settings of Sir Walter Scott's The Lady of the Lake, in which Ellen prays to the Virgin Mary. Because it begins with the words of the Latin prayer, it is now known as Schubert's "Ave Maria."

**Wanderer Fantasy**
Schubert's virtuosic C major Fantasy for solo piano, based on his song "Der Wanderer." It was so difficult that Schubert himself could not play it, reportedly saying "the devil may play it," and Liszt later transcribed it for piano and orchestra.

**Piano Sonata in B-flat major (D. 960)**
Schubert's last piano sonata, written in the final months of his life in 1828. Early in its first movement, an ominous low trill on G-flat interrupts the serene theme and foreshadows a striking modulation away from B-flat major.

**String Quintet in C major**
Schubert's only string quintet, written in 1828, which adds a second cello to the standard string quartet. It is one of his final masterpieces.

**"Tragic" Symphony (Symphony No. 4 in C minor)**
An early Schubert symphony that he himself nicknamed "Tragic." It is often clued alongside his "Little" C major Sixth Symphony.

**Schubertiades and Johann Michael Vogl**
Schubertiades were informal Viennese gatherings devoted to Schubert's music, famously depicted by his friend Moritz von Schwind. The baritone Johann Michael Vogl championed his songs during his lifetime, and the 20th-century baritone Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau became the most famous interpreter of his more than 600 lieder.
